newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore offshore insurer prospects tough - report.
newsitem.headline: Singapore offshore insurer prospects tough - report.

text.p: The prospects for offshore insurance business in Singapore remain poor as regional competition intensifies, Singapore's Insurance Commissioner said on Tuesday.
"Growth prospects of offshore general business remain weak," Lim Shu Chiau said in her annual report for the year to December 31, 1996.
"Market conditions are expected to be difficult as the increased availability of reinsurance capacity worldwide would intensify competition and drive rates down," she added.
For the second successive year reinsurers reported a fall in offshore underwriting, with gross premiums slipping 0.9 percent to Singapore $713.8 million from S$720.4 million in 1995.
"I've seen no real growth for the past two years and I don't see any coming either," said one senior manager at an international reinsurer.
"Low or no growth will be a feature of the market for some time to come," he added.
Lim said the fall was due to "trimming of unprofitable business and a general softening of premium rates".

The drop was shallower than the 3.7 per recorded in 1995, with reinsurance premiums -- which account for about 61 percent of offshore business in the city state -- buoyed by the arrival of new writers.
The number of authorised reinsurers as of January 1, 1997 rose to 43 from 38 previously and the number has swelled subsequently with the award of licences to Lincoln National Re and CNA Re.
But direct insurers saw their offshore business surge 19 percent to S$198.5 million from S$166.8 million.
"Unlike the reinsurers, from our point of view the prospects for offshore business are good," said a spokeswoman for Allianz Singapore, the local unit of German giant Allianz AG.
"The environment here is competitive of course, but not negatively so on the direct side," she added.
Lim's report showed life business to be the healthiest insurance sector in Singapore.
Annual premium business jumped 12.4 percent to S$656.7 million from S$584.5 million and single premiums leapt 26.8 percent to S$699.5 million from S$551.5 million.
Total business in force rose 17.3 percent to S$3.5 billion.

The main driver for life business came from reforms to Singapore's compulsory Central Provident Fund (CPF) savings scheme which permitted investment of savings in a range of investment-linked insurance products.
The further reform of CPF rules from January 1, 1997 was seen by the industry as key to improving prospects for the year.
"Prospects for growth remain good, fuelled particularly by the CPF investment scheme," said Tan Beng Lee, chief executive of Singapore's biggest life player, Great Eastern Life.

His assessment was echoed by American International Assurance, the biggest foreign life insurer in Singapore, which expects a large part of its growth "to be derived from the CPF investment scheme", according to a spokesman.
-- Singapore newsroom 65-8703080
